solutionSteps: \textnormal{Coefficient comparison gives }F(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\frac{1}{2}^{n(n-1)/2}}{n!}z^n.\textnormal{The ratio test proves entire convergence and all coefficients are positive.}

\textnormal{Write }L=\ln r,\quad c=\ln 2>0.\textnormal{Ignoring the factorial only for an upper bound, complete the square in }nL-\frac c2n(n-1).\textnormal{The resulting discrete Gaussian sum is bounded by a constant depending only on c, times }\exp\left(\frac{(L+c/2)^2}{2c}\right).

\textnormal{For the lower bound retain the single term with }n=\lfloor L/c\rfloor.\textnormal{Its logarithm is }\frac{L^2}{2c}+O(L\ln L),\textnormal{because }0\le\ln(n!)\le n\ln n.\textnormal{Divide both bounds by the square of L.}
statement: \textnormal{Let F be the entire solution of }F\prime(z)=F(z/2),\quad F(0)=1.\textnormal{For positive real r, find }\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\ln F(r)}{(\ln r)^2}.

analyticCertificate: The coefficient ratio is |z|q^n/(n+1), tending to zero for every fixed z, proving existence and uniqueness among entire solutions. For the upper estimate, the sum of exp(-c(n-center)^2/2) over integer n is uniformly bounded over all centers by a constant plus its Gaussian integral. The lower index differs from L/c by less than one, so its quadratic exponent differs from L squared/(2c) by O(L); the factorial bound costs only O(L ln L). These two analytic estimates prove the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Coefficient comparison gives }F(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\frac{1}{5}^{n(n-1)/2}}{n!}z^n.\textnormal{The ratio test proves entire convergence and all coefficients are positive.}

\textnormal{Write }L=\ln r,\quad c=\ln 5>0.\textnormal{Ignoring the factorial only for an upper bound, complete the square in }nL-\frac c2n(n-1).\textnormal{The resulting discrete Gaussian sum is bounded by a constant depending only on c, times }\exp\left(\frac{(L+c/2)^2}{2c}\right).

\textnormal{For the lower bound retain the single term with }n=\lfloor L/c\rfloor.\textnormal{Its logarithm is }\frac{L^2}{2c}+O(L\ln L),\textnormal{because }0\le\ln(n!)\le n\ln n.\textnormal{Divide both bounds by the square of L.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For a proposed peak M, the endpoint constraints are }\int_0^{1}u\,\mathrm dt=0,\quad\int_0^{1}(1-t)u(t)\,\mathrm dt=1.
\textnormal{With the first integral fixed, the second is largest when u equals M as early as possible and minus M afterward. The switch is }\tau=\frac12\left(1+\frac{0}M\right).

\textnormal{The requested displacement exceeds the midpoint value. Equating it to this upper bound and choosing the positive quadratic root gives M. The corresponding switch lies inside the time interval and realizes both endpoints.}
statement: x\prime\prime=u(t),\quad x(0)=x\prime(0)=0,\quad x(1)=1,\quad x\prime(1)=0.\textnormal{Among real measurable essentially bounded accelerations, find the smallest possible essential supremum of the absolute acceleration.}

analyticCertificate: For fixed M and the mean constraint, compare any admissible control with the two-level control at tau. The integral of their difference is zero, and (Tend-t)-(Tend-tau) has the same sign as the saturated control difference, so the weighted displacement difference is nonnegative. This proves the extremal bound without assuming a control theorem. The positive quadratic root is at least |V|/Tend and is strictly larger in the stated regime, so the switch is feasible. The explicit saturated control attains the minimum.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The map }w=\frac z{z-1}\textnormal{ is conformal and bijective from the domain onto the circular annulus }1/3<|w|<1/2.
\textnormal{Under a conformal coordinate change, gradient length squared and area have reciprocal scale factors. Thus Dirichlet energy is unchanged.}
\textnormal{For each angle, the boundary difference is one. Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz gives }1\le\left(\int_{1/3}^{1/2}\rho\,u_\rho^2\,\mathrm d\rho\right)\ln(\frac{3}{2}).
\textnormal{Integrate over angles and discard the nonnegative angular energy. Equality is attained by }u(z)=\frac{\ln\!\left(3\left|z/(z-1)\right|\right)}{\ln(\frac{3}{2})}.
statement: \textnormal{In the complex plane define }\Omega=\left\{z:\frac1{3}<\left|\frac z{z-1}\right|<\frac1{2}\right\}.\textnormal{For real continuously differentiable functions on the closure, equal to zero on the inner ratio boundary and one on the outer ratio boundary, find the minimum of }\iint_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,\mathrm dA.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{1}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}
statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(\frac{1}{2}n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{1n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}
statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(1n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{2n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}
statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(2n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The polynomial is a monic generalized Laguerre polynomial. Rodrigues integration by parts shows orthogonality against every polynomial of degree below its degree for the positive weight }t^{\frac{7}{2}n}e^{-t}\quad(t>0).

\textnormal{All roots are positive and simple: otherwise the product of the positive sign-changing factors would have lower degree and its weighted inner product with the polynomial would have one strict sign, contradicting orthogonality.}
\textnormal{At the fixed negative argument, positive roots give uniform bounds }-1\le F_n(-1)<0,\qquad |F_n\prime(-1)|\le1.
\textnormal{Every convergent subsequence must therefore approach the unique nonnegative root of this quadratic. Compactness then gives convergence of the entire sequence.}
statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(\frac{7}{2}n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?

analyticCertificate: Rodrigues formula is proportional to t^(-alpha)e^t times the nth derivative of e^(-t)t^(n+alpha), with alpha=cn>0. Integrating against t^j for j<n transfers all n derivatives and gives zero; boundary terms vanish at both endpoints. The standard sign-change polynomial argument then proves n distinct positive roots. At z=-1 each resolvent term has magnitude at most one and each derivative term at most one, giving the explicit uniform error bound. The negative algebraic root is excluded by S_n>=0; uniqueness on [0,1] plus compactness proves the limit.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Scale the turning point and make the logarithmic-derivative substitution: }t=\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{5}}s,\quad y_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\frac{3}{5}}Y(s),\quad Y=-u\prime/u.
\textnormal{The substitution }u(v)=\sqrt v\,W(z)\textnormal{ gives the modified Bessel equation }z^2W\prime\prime+zW\prime-(z^2+\nu^2)W=0.

\textnormal{The negative attracting asymptotic selects the positive recessive solution }u(v)=\sqrt v\,K_\nu(z).\textnormal{ Here }K_\nu\textnormal{ denotes the exponentially decaying real solution of the modified Bessel equation, up to its standard normalization.}

extnormal{The two leading powers in its small positive argument expansion give }u(v)=A+Bv+o(v),\quad A=	frac12\Gamma(
u)(5)^
u,\quad B=	frac12\Gamma(-
u)(5)^{-
u}.

extnormal{The derivative with respect to scaled time has the opposite sign from the derivative in the positive variable. Hence }Y(0)= rac BA=(5)^{-2
u} rac{\Gamma(-
u)}{\Gamma(
u)}=-(5)^{1-2
u} rac{\Gamma(1-
u)}{\Gamma(
u)}.
\textnormal{The scaling is exact, so this is also the normalized limit in the question.}
statement: \textnormal{For each positive }\varepsilon,\textnormal{ let }y_\varepsilon\textnormal{ be the real solution on the negative half-line selected by the displayed asymptotic condition, continued to zero. Find the limit. The Gamma function is defined by the displayed integral.}\quad\varepsilon y_\varepsilon\prime=t^{3}+y_\varepsilon^2,\qquad \frac{y_\varepsilon(t)}{-(-t)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\longrightarrow1\quad(t\to-\infty),\qquad\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\varepsilon^{-\frac{3}{5}}y_\varepsilon(0)=?,\quad\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du\ (a>0).

analyticCertificate: For v>0 the linear equation is u_vv-v^n u=0. The modified-Bessel substitution is verified coefficientwise. The positive recessive K solution behaves like a positive multiple of z^(-1/2)exp(-z); its logarithmic derivative has the required negative Riccati asymptotic. Any nonzero growing I component gives the opposite leading logarithmic-derivative sign, so the branch is unique up to an irrelevant multiplier. Positivity prevents poles on negative time. For 0<nu<1, the exact connection K_nu=pi*(I_-nu-I_nu)/(2 sin(pi nu)) and the entire defining I series give the two displayed powers, with a differentiable remainder o(v); higher terms have powers at least n+2. The constant A is positive, so continuation to zero is regular. Gamma recurrence converts the negative Gamma argument to the positive arguments explicitly defined in the prompt.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Factor P(z)=(z-1)\textasciicircum{}2 Q(z), with Q(z)=sum\_(j=0)\textasciicircum{}(m-2)(m-1-j)z\textasciicircum{}j. The coefficients of Q(Rw), R=1+1/m, are positive and strictly decreasing.}

\begin{gathered}\textnormal{A polynomial with positive}\\\textnormal{nonincreasing coefficients has}\\\textnormal{no zero in |w|<1: multiply by}\\\textnormal{1-w; the sum of all}\\\textnormal{nonconstant coefficient}\\\textnormal{magnitudes equals the}\\\textnormal{constant, and strict radius}\\\textnormal{makes triangle inequality}\\\textnormal{strict. Apply the same}\\\textnormal{argument at a slightly larger}\\\textnormal{R, still below (m-1)/(m-2).}\end{gathered}

\begin{gathered}\textnormal{Thus Q has no zeros in or on}\\\textnormal{the circle |z|=R, and P has}\\\textnormal{exactly its double root at one}\\\textnormal{inside. Argument principle}\\\textnormal{gives winding number two, so}\\\textnormal{the real circulation is 4pi.}\end{gathered}
